content.overview: Pre-use checks help catch obvious equipment problems before they create injury, crop loss, poor process performance or unnecessary downtime.

vocabulary.definition: A defined inspection performed before operating equipment to confirm obvious readiness and safety conditions.
A condition that must be met before an asset is used for the assigned task.
A controlled status indicating equipment should not be used until authorized evaluation or release.

sections.title: Check the asset before use
sections.body: Routine checks may include asset identity, cleanliness, visible damage, leaks, hoses or connections, guards, protective features, indicators and other steps defined by the equipment manufacturer or facility procedure. The exact checklist depends on the asset.

sections.title: Do not bypass protective features
sections.body: A missing guard, damaged cord, abnormal leak, unsafe condition or other failed readiness criterion triggers the facility's out-of-service or escalation process. Finishing the task is not justification for bypassing a protective device.

workedExamples: A leaking irrigation connection is handled only through the approved operator response or maintenance escalation.
A missing guard prevents use even if the operator believes careful technique would avoid contact.
commonMistakes: Skipping checks because equipment worked on the previous shift.
Using an improvised repair in place of an authorized maintenance decision.
content.practicalApplication: Perform a simulated pre-use inspection and classify findings as acceptable, routine operator correction, out-of-service/escalation or emergency hazard.
content.summary: Technicians verify equipment readiness before use and refuse to bypass failed safeguards, damaged equipment or authorization boundaries.

blocks.title: Pre-use checks protect both safety and process reliability
blocks.body: A readiness check is not a full maintenance inspection. It is the defined operator-level review performed before use to catch obvious conditions that make an asset unsafe, unavailable, dirty, incorrectly configured, or unreliable for the assigned task. The exact checklist comes from the equipment instructions and facility procedure.

items.title: Confirm the asset
items.body: Verify the equipment identity and that it is the asset assigned for the work.

items.title: Check controlled status
items.body: Look for out-of-service tags, open faults, holds, prior-shift notes, or other status information that affects use.

items.title: Inspect accessible condition
items.body: Use the assigned external check for cleanliness, visible damage, leaks, hoses/connections, guards/covers, obstructions, and other specified readiness points.

items.title: Review indicators
items.body: Check permitted readings, alarms, displays, or readiness indicators called out by the procedure.

items.title: Classify the finding
items.body: Decide whether the asset is ready, needs an approved routine operator correction, must remain out of service and be escalated, or presents an emergency hazard.

blocks.alt: Diagram separating routine operator care that is explicitly assigned by the manual and site procedure from skilled servicing such as removing guards, entering hazardous motion areas, opening protected electrical components, disassembling powered equipment, or releasing stored energy.
blocks.caption: A failed readiness check does not authorize the technician to cross from inspection into servicing.

blocks.title: The guard is missing but the task is behind schedule
blocks.setting: A powered piece of equipment passes its normal indicator check, but a required guard is missing. A coworker says careful hand placement makes it safe enough for one short run.
blocks.prompt: What is the correct Technician I response?
options: Run it once at reduced speed
Do not use the asset; follow the out-of-service/escalation process for the failed readiness criterion
Replace the guard with a temporary improvised cover
blocks.answer: Do not use the asset; follow the out-of-service/escalation process for the failed readiness criterion.
blocks.feedback: A failed protective feature is not corrected by careful technique, extra PPE, or an improvised substitute unless a controlled authorized process specifically provides for that action.

blocks.title: Pre-use readiness checklist record
blocks.description: The checklist should capture the asset and the actual findings rather than a generic 'checked' statement.

fields.label: Status before check
fields.value: Available, tagged, open fault, prior-shift note, or other controlled status

fields.label: Assigned inspection points
fields.value: Guard, cover, hose/connection, leak, damage, cleanliness, obstruction, indicator, or other asset-specific criteria

fields.label: Observed condition
fields.value: What was actually seen or read

fields.label: Operator correction
fields.value: Only the routine action explicitly allowed by the procedure, if any

fields.label: Final readiness
fields.value: Ready, out of service, escalated, or emergency response

fields.label: Notification / ticket
fields.value: Required person, role, or maintenance record

blocks.title: Perform a simulated pre-use inspection
blocks.instructions: Inspect a mock equipment packet containing asset images, status tags, readings, and an operator checklist. Classify every finding without performing unauthorized repair work.
prompts: Verify the asset identity and prior status.
Identify each readiness criterion that passes or fails.
Separate routine operator corrections from out-of-service conditions.
Identify the finding that crosses into maintenance or hazardous-energy servicing.
Write the final readiness status and escalation note.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Pre-use competence means finding problems before use and respecting the response boundary. A failed check is a reason to control the asset—not a license to improvise a repair.
